chapter: Philadelphia concerts and Jelly Roll Morton
title: Meeting Jelly Roll Morton in Philadelphia and Washington
summary: Rose first saw Morton in a Philadelphia theater band in 1937-38, then visited him regularly at the Jungle Inn in Washington over five or six months.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Remembering Jelly Roll Morton: the man, the band

blocks.x: So, what about, uh, Jolly Roll Morton? I'm skipping about. Excuse me.

All right. Mm-hmm. Well, I met Jolly Roll Morton the first time, uh, now, let's see, that's gotta be in nineteen thirty-seven, and, or maybe thirty-eight. I don't know, but it was in the winter at that time. Mm-hmm. I was introduced to Jolly Roll by Rhys Dupree, who, uh, claimed to have been, and may well have been, the composer of Shorten and Bread and Dupree Blues. And it was in a, in a hotel called the Douglas Hotel on Broad and Lombard Street in Philadelphia. I had seen Jolly Roll at the Lincoln Theater either that day or the day before, saw the band, and found it singularly unimpressive, and, uh, went backstage, uh, to see somebody. I don't recall who. I passed Jolly Roll in the car. And, uh, we nodded to each other as strangers, and, uh, had no idea who he was. I mean, he had no idea who I was at the time. And, uh, uh, I was in, having a drink with Rhys Dupree in the hotel while he was trying to convince me to join him in, or actually to finance a promotion that he had afoot, or wanted to have afoot. And in the process, Jolly Roll came in, and we were at the, and, uh, the next time I saw him was definitely in 1938, and that was, uh, at the Jungle, and I first went to Washington for the purpose of being a delegate to the Keep America Out of War convention. And I was on a panel there with, uh, Smedley Butler and John Dooley. And, uh, uh, since I knew that Jolly Roll was there, and that he had this place called The Jungle Inn, I went up. And the first night I went up there, uh, it was about 9.30 to 10 o'clock, and nobody was there but Jolly Roll. And, uh, I asked him, is the place open? He says, yeah, it's open. He said, but you wouldn't know it. And, uh, so he sat down and played, and I had a few drinks, and he had a few drinks, and we talked. And, uh, I stayed there until 3 or 3.30 in the morning. Nobody ever did come in. And, uh, I came in the next night and the next night, and then I took to going in there regularly. And, uh, in fact, uh, I began to make regular trips from Philadelphia to Washington, bringing people with me to see him then, and listen to him talk and play the piano. Uh, and that went on over a period of five or six months.
The first time you heard him there was when you were with Reece Dupree?
Oh, he wasn't playing then. He just came in, you know, into the hotel. Yeah, but he was at the theater. He was at the Lincoln Theater.
